name: Photolithographic diffusion windows
summary: Andrus and Bond used light-sensitive resist to etch precise windows in silicon oxide before adding dopants, a patterning method Fairchild soon used in transistor production.
description: Jules Andrus and Walter Bond adapted photoresist patterning to etch windows in silicon oxide before localized diffusion.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Photoresist patterning, already used in printing and photoengraving, was adapted to define small regions on silicon.

events.statement: Fairchild used photolithographic oxide-window fabrication in its mesa transistor work and shipped 100 2N696 transistors by 1958.
events.scope: Fairchild’s photoresist-patterned silicon-oxide openings used to delimit diffusion in mesa transistor fabrication; individual masks need not be identical to the earlier Bell Labs masks.
events.caveats: The Fairchild method is contextual evidence of use of the same general patterned oxide-window process; the source does not identify every original Bell mask or prove exact transfer of a physical tool.

evidence.supports: Moore describes photoresist and oxide openings, Fairchild’s mesa emitter diffusion, and 100 early 2N696 shipments in 1958.
